Industry observers note that withdrawals will close at 08:00 UTC on 31st December 2026. KuCoin reserves the right to close them earlier over project-related problems, with the exchange also warning that stablecoin conversion of remaining balances won’t be guaranteed.

At press time, CoinGecko highlighted $90.42 million in combined 24-hour volumes across KuCoin’s XMR/USDT and XMR/USDC pairs. Together, they accounted for 50.27% of Monero’s spot trading volume.

Including XMR/BTC and XMR/ETH, that brought KuCoin’s total to $104.60 million or 58.14%.

Hence, the question: Where could that trading move now? At the time of writing, the remaining exchanges showed more buy orders close to the market price, despite reporting a lower turnover.

Recent findings suggest that kraken’s XMR/USD pair had approximately $386,970 in buy orders within 2% below its price, compared to KuCoin’s XMR/USDT pair’s $85,683. WhiteBIT and HTX’s XMR/USDT pairs showed $260,810 and $196,231, respectively.

That gave Kraken roughly 4.5 times KuCoin’s nearby buying depth, with WhiteBIT and HTX also offering larger buy-side cushions. These orders could help absorb selling, although traders could cancel them at any time.

That access problem extended into services marketed as alternatives to CEXs.

Dash’s Joel Valenzuela also raised a similar concern. He warned that further CEX losses could make no-KYC Monero swaps harder to obtain.

Finally, Cake Wallet founder Vik Sharma also directed users towards wallet-based swaps, writing,.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Trendsetter News » Midnight Savings Launch Puts NIGHT Ahead Of ADA.

Monument Bank’s Midnight rollout links banking activity more directly to NIGHT than ADA, but its £250M bid reflects initial capacity.

The £250 million figure attached to Monument Bank’s Midnight rollout is an initial capacity limit, not confirmed customer deposits, according to a video from crypto commentator FireHustle.

That distinction sits at the heart of the host’s analysis: a bank adopting technology built by Cardano’s developers does not necessarily translate into immediate demand for ADA.

The video describes a savings product that keeps customers’ money in pounds while recording their accounts on Midnight, the privacy-focused blockchain developed by Input Output.

Its potential significance lies less in the headline amount than in which token benefits from the activity.

According to Fire Hustle, Monument’s offering pays existing customers a fixed 5.2% for one year. Account details remain private, and customers cannot sell or transfer the blockchain records, even to another Monument customer.

Cardano’s Founder Charles Hoskinson celebrated the rollout with the phrase “250 million pounds on-chain.” But the host says Monument has not disclosed actual deposits, despite tokens representing the full initial allocation already having been created.

The YouTube video also cites Midnight Foundation president Fahmi Syed saying seven other banks are considering similar products: six in Canada and one in Japan.

Canada merits attention because Calgary-based digital-asset custodian Balance handles Monument’s tokens, according to the video. The host explicitly cautions against assuming the unnamed institutions are Canada’s six largest banks.

Recent findings suggest that midnight’s token structure is the investment question. The video states holding NIGHT generates DUST, the resource used to pay network transaction fees. Banks or service providers can therefore cover customers’ activity without requiring savers to handle tokens themselves.

Industry observers note that “Somebody still has to hold the Night that makes the Dust,” she notes. That creates a more direct connection between Midnight usage and NIGHT than between that usage and ADA, although additional activity does not guarantee token-price gains.

The ADA connection is more distant. Cardano stake-pool operators are expected to help secure Midnight in early 2027, with potential rewards extending to their ADA delegators. Those rewards are prospective, not existing income.

Recent findings suggest that fire Hustle reports ADA trading more than 90% below its peak at recording. However, the more useful indicators are actual Monument deposits, transaction volumes and confirmed bank launches.

The cashier also shows a minimum for each coin and network, and LIQD’s terms say a deposit below it is not credited. A transfer to the wrong address or network may not be recoverable, since a blockchain transfer cannot be stopped once it has been sent.

LIQD takes deposits in crypto only, and USD, EUR and CAD serve as display currencies. The figure shown in those currencies moves with the coin’s market price.

In a recent development, at a Bitcoin price of $80,000, a balance of 0.01 BTC reveals as $800. If the price drops to $76,000, the same 0.01 BTC shows as $760 without a single bet in between.

Sources indicate that to withdraw, players select a coin and network in the cashier and enter their wallet address. LIQD’s terms do not specify a fixed processing time. Withdrawals are subject to verification and regulatory review, and larger amounts undergo manual review.

Each Originals round combines a server seed, a client seed that the player controls, and a nonce.

Sources indicate that once the server seed is revealed, the player can reproduce the result with the Seeds and Verify controls built into the games. LIQD states that its Originals have been audited by the Provably Fair Foundation. Slots, live tables and other third-party games run on their providers’ own systems and fall outside this verification.

Sources indicate that LIQD’s VIP program has 31 levels across ten tiers. Progress depends on the total amount wagered, measured in US dollars. The starting tier, Water, includes instant rakeback. Later tiers offer benefits such as weekly and monthly bonuses, subject to the terms of each offer.

In a recent development, LIQD Ltd is registered in Belize under company number 000052980. Its licence, ALSI-202603048-FI2, was issued by the Government of the Autonomous Island of Anjouan, Union of Comoros, and Return to Player Ltd in Cyprus acts as payment agent.

The terms list the US, the UK, France, the Netherlands, Spain, Austria, Cyprus, Comoros, and FATF high-risk call-for-action jurisdictions as restricted. LIQD runs risk-based AML and KYC checks, and verification may be requested.

Tether’s USDT led stablecoin borrowing on Aave, Fluid and Spark in a July 30 snapshot published by the European Banking Authority (EBA) on Nov. 25.

The EBA renewed its call for the European Commission to assess rules for firms that give customers access to decentralized lending, including possible restrictions on loans involving stablecoins that lack the required EU authorization.

Sources indicate that in its comparison of six lending protocols, the regulator grouped USDT and its USDT0 bridged version when describing demand on Aave, Fluid and Spark. The EBA also found that borrowers on JustLend overwhelmingly favored USDT and pointed to the token’s dominance on the Tron blockchain.

USDC accounted for a larger share of active loans than USDT on Compound and Morpho.

The EBA measured each stablecoin against all active loans on the same protocol. Separate estimates suggest EU participation in decentralized finance remains limited, and self-hosted wallets and reporting gaps make it difficult to identify where users are based.

The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) requires authorization for covered stablecoins to be offered to the public or admitted to trading in the EU, and USDT lacks that authorization.

The EBA’s summary of MiCA’s scope says fully decentralized services operating without an intermediary fall outside the rules. The report says some EU consumers may hold stablecoins like USDT in wallets they control themselves.

Some crypto firms give customers access to lending protocols through their own interfaces, while others offer products tied to decentralized lending.

The EBA describes arrangements that let customers put their stablecoins to work without opening a self-hosted wallet. In those cases, customers depend on the platform that handles the investment.

Some firms connect customers to lending protocols through an interface. Others offer products tied to those markets.

A firm can serve as the entry point even when the lending protocol is decentralized.

In a recent development, the diagram shows access routes and a recommendation for assessment. Line weight does not show loan volume.

The flow diagram summarizes the access routes in section 3.3 of the EBA report and connects the firm route to the recommendation reiterated on Nov. 25.

The diagram demonstrates access routes and a recommendation for assessment. Line weight does not show loan volume.

Recent findings suggest that the EBA raised the issue in September as part of the Commission’s MiCA review, warning the Commission to weigh the costs and benefits of additional requirements for intermediaries. The options include checking whether products suit customers, requiring more disclosures, and limiting leverage.

The Commission could also assess restrictions on firms that facilitate borrowing and lending in stablecoins such as USDT, which require authorization but lack it.

In a recent development, the November report reiterates a recommendation for the MiCA review. The EBA aims to continue monitoring decentralized finance in 2027, including how consumers access stablecoins that lack MiCA authorization. That work could inform any further advice to the Commission.

That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig declared the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

Recent findings suggest that if you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we revealed a first investment of around € 3b in a new manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the new production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla plans to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company states it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

Sources indicate that it leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the newly introduced hall will be bigger than the original factory.

The building isn’t fresh. Tesla laid out a initiative to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only remarked the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

In a recent development, giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the new hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

The EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

It has been revealed that tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

In a recent development, rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Sources indicate that tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Industry observers note that tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

It has been revealed that the Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU said no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

It has been revealed that and the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

According to recent reports, that’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

In a recent development, this is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

It has been revealed that good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Sources indicate that will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Trendsetter News » Analyst: Ripple’s Growth Doesn’t Guarantee $10 XRP.

Ripple’s expansion alone won’t send XRP to $10, a popular wealth coach states.

A $10 XRP would imply a circulating market value of roughly $630 billion, not simply another rally on Ripple announcements.

In a recent development, that is the central argument from Dr. Kamilah Stevenson, a wealth coach whose latest YouTube video episode examines why the company’s institutional expansion has not translated into the token price many holders expected.

In a recent development, using approximately 63 billion XRP in circulation, Stevenson argues that reaching that XRP valuation requires more than partnerships and regulatory milestones. It requires sustained demand to own the token, rather than merely move money through it.

Stevenson separates Ripple’s corporate performance, adoption of its products, demand for XRP and the token’s market price. Those categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable: a customer using Ripple’s custody services or stablecoin does not necessarily need XRP.

Even payments routed through XRP may generate limited lasting demand. In the process she describes, a payment provider buys the token, transfers it and sells it into the destination currency within seconds, allowing the same inventory to support repeated transactions.

Sources indicate that “Major payment numbers alone don’t automatically push the price up,” Dr. Stevenson states. The more consequential question is how much XRP participants need to keep available between transactions.

According to recent reports, market makers may hold inventory to support larger payment flows, creating a potential link between usage and ownership. Still, the video does not quantify how much additional inventory those flows would require.

Industry observers note that dr. Kamilah Stevenson cites roughly 1.19 billion XRP held by ETFs and about 473 million held by Evernorth, a company established to accumulate XRP. Those are figures presented in the video, rather than independently verified current totals.

Her distinction is useful: XRP-backed fund holdings represent direct token ownership, while the national trust bank approval she attributes to Ripple does not itself require institutions to purchase XRP.

It has been revealed that supply remains part of the calculation. Stevenson puts Ripple’s escrow holdings at around 31 billion XRP, with up to one billion released monthly and unused amounts returned to escrow. An unlock is therefore not equivalent to an immediate market sale.

Recent findings suggest that the sharper test is whether an announcement creates incremental buying, how long those tokens stay held and whether newly introduced supply offsets that demand. Dr. Stevenson remains bullish, but the adoption figures she discusses do not establish when XRP reaches $10.

Recent findings suggest that traders are placing more bets on Bitcoin’s price falling. At press time, put options were high at strike levels of $60K, $58K, $50K and $40K. Generally then, with the growing put/call ratio and elevated short interest, it would seem that traders may be bracing for further downside. They might not be anticipating a swift rebound either.

In short, Bitcoin is showing early signs of a potential bottom. However, shrinking stablecoin liquidity, record ETF outflows, and rising demand for downside protection allude to the presence of bearish pressure. Cardano is already looking beyond its upcoming Dijkstra hard fork, with Euler emerging as the next major upgrade.

In a recent release, Intersect, a member-based organization in the Cardano ecosystem, said it is planning the next Cardano upgrade, Euler, with the first meeting of the Euler Scoping Working Group scheduled for December 1, 2026, at 5 p.m. UTC. Here, participants will contribute to early discussions on the scope of the next Cardano era.

Recent findings suggest that the development signals Cardano's continued commitment to evolving its blockchain infrastructure through a structured upgrade process. While Dijkstra represents the current focus, discussions on Euler will set the tone for what comes next for the network.

In a recent development, the Dijkstra era delivers Cardano's major protocol upgrade in two phases: Phase 1, Dijkstra hard fork (Protocol Version 12), introduces the Dijkstra ledger era and ships Ouroboros Linear Leios as a complete, activated feature. The second phase activates Ouroboros Peras via an intra-era hard fork. Peras is a settlement-speed upgrade that adds a voting overlay to the existing Ouroboros Praos chain selection rule.

Recent findings suggest that as of the latest revision by Intersect, Dijkstra ledger features are currently being tested on DijkstraNet, while Linear Leios consensus and throughput are being tested on MusashiNet. Both are converging toward Node 11.3, which is the target hard fork release candidate.

According to recent reports, the Dijkstra upgrade requires both constitutional and technical changes in the era of on-chain governance. Discussions and refinements on constitutional guardrails (Enhancement Constitution) or CAP-12 "Dijkstra era parameters" continue on the Constitutional Amendment Portal ahead of Mainnet submission.

It has been revealed that protocol Version 12 has already gone live on Musashi and DijkstraNet, while a hard fork release candidate (11.3) is required for Preview and Preprod hard forks. In its recent post, Intersect sets the Dijkstra hard fork target timeline as December 2026 for the Preview network, including the Update Constitution and hard fork.

On-chain activation of the Update Constitution action on the mainnet is expected in December 2026, while the Dijkstra hard fork is expected in Q1 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ethereum’s core developers kept a proposal to curb transaction censorship on the schedule for an upgrade called Hegotá at their Nov. 26 meeting.

They deferred a final decision while client teams considered whether the work could run alongside efforts to make the network’s consensus system resistant to quantum attacks.

The proposal, known as FOCIL, remains Hegotá’s lead consensus change. The All Core Devs call record puts the next review of the fork’s scope around Dec. 10.

It has been revealed that under draft EIP-7805, a committee of validators would broadcast lists of transactions waiting in the public queue. Validators that vote on the next block would check the lists they received before a cutoff.

If a builder leaves out a listed transaction that is still valid at the end of the block and fits in the remaining gas, those validators would withhold their votes. They would ignore lists from a committee member they saw send conflicting versions.

For someone whose eligible transaction makes a timely list, a builder’s decision to leave it out could cost that block its votes.

EthPandaOps’ October Heze devnet initiative carried forward tests of list propagation, timing, and how inclusion lists interact with the separation of block builders and proposers.

Sources indicate that the team kept Frame Transactions, another Hegotá proposal, on a separate test track. The proposed Bogotá devnet would focus on execution-layer testing while teams wait for a decision before running a combined test.

FOCIL co-author Jihoon Song argues that developers and testers can move inclusion lists toward release while researchers work on post-quantum decoupled consensus, a redesign of how Ethereum agrees on blocks.

He would start with preregistration so validators can register new keys ahead of a switch in how they sign. Song expects most FOCIL work to be done by the time the consensus design is ready for client teams to implement for mainnet.

It has been revealed that at the Nov. 24 post-quantum breakout, developers discussed how to restore a test network that stalled after some clients took too long to generate new validator keys. The test is part of the early consensus work the Ethereum Foundation described in its Nov. 23 revision.

Ethlabs researcher Caspar Schwarz-Schilling argues that a small group of researchers and client developers with a broad view of Ethereum would be needed to deliver both changes safely.

He favors deferring FOCIL so that group can focus on consensus. The extent of the overlap depends in part on what developers expect the first version of FOCIL to handle.

Two proposals discussed on Nov. 26 would put FOCIL at different points in Ethereum’s transition to quantum-safe consensus.

The timing decision affects how soon eligible public transactions could gain stronger protection against being left out.

According to recent reports, the paths show proposed sequencing. They convey no duration, staffing commitment or final fork decision.

The diagram maps proposals made on Nov. 26 and the shared integration questions described in the draft inclusion-list specification and Song’s compatibility analysis.

According to recent reports, the paths show proposed sequencing. They convey no duration, staffing commitment or final fork decision.

The FOCIL draft relies on BLS signatures to authenticate the lists themselves, and those signatures would eventually need a quantum-resistant replacement.

In a separate technical analysis, Song also identifies work on how lists would carry larger post-quantum transactions or the proofs that could accompany them without overloading the network.

The decoupled consensus design also leaves open which group of validators would enforce the lists.

Barnabas Busa proposed a narrower version that would enforce inclusion for certain existing transaction types and excuse builders from including Frame Transactions.

Inclusion lists could then protect owners of those existing transaction types in Hegotá, while users of Frame Transactions would have to wait for enforcement to cover them.

According to recent reports, the next post-quantum consensus session is scheduled for Nov. 27 at 14:00 UTC. When developers return to Hegotá’s scope, the practical test is how much work the first version needs from the people designing the upcoming consensus system.

BYD is bringing its $10,000 ‘Great’ Seagull overseas, but it won’t replace the Dolphin Surf

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD’s newly introduced, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.
  • Sources indicate that the Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China.
  • With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD’s newly introduced, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

Sources indicate that the Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

In China, the newly introduced Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

According to recent reports, the second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s newly introduced Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the new version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

It has been revealed that with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

Inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The latest setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

The optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

In China, BYD offers the new Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

Industry observers note that the current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1165 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger.
  • Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and states it has the car’s event data recorder and video.
  • According to recent reports, at 11:43 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators notes Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and states it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

According to recent reports, at 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

The SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

FHP mentioned the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

Recent findings suggest that it identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

This record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it notes Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

Industry observers note that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

So Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

Autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s notable to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

It has been revealed that there’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

It has been revealed that this is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a upcoming record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

According to recent reports, this is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

Tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

We’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

It has been revealed that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

Strategic Bitcoin Reserve Bill Clears House Committee, Heads to Floor

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A bill that would write the U.S.
  • In a recent development, the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, H.R.
  • Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, introduced the bill on May 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A bill that would write the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve into federal law is now eligible for a vote on the House floor, after the House Financial Services Committee formally reported it on Tuesday.

In a recent development, the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, H.R. 8957, was filed with amendments as House Report 119-894 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789 on Nov. 24, according to congressional records. The committee had voted 28-21 to advance the bill at a Sept. 16 markup.

Sources indicate that rep. Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, introduced the bill on May 21. It now lists 23 cosponsors, including Rep. Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat, with Reps. Byron Donalds and Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida added on Nov. 24.

The reported text directs the Treasury secretary to set up a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile within 180 days of the law taking effect. Bitcoin owned by the federal government would move into the reserve, while other digital assets would go to the stockpile.

Recent findings suggest that the centerpiece is a lock-up. Treasury would have to hold all bitcoin deposited in the reserve for at least 20 years after enactment, and during that period no reserve bitcoin could be “sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of for any purpose.”.

After the 20 years, the Treasury secretary could recommend selling up to 10% of the reserve in any two-year period. Two years before the holding period ends, Treasury would have to send Congress recommendations on whether to keep holding or begin a gradual release.

Industry observers note that federal agencies would have 60 days after enactment to give Treasury a full accounting of the bitcoin and other digital assets they hold or have seized. Until the reserve is set up, agencies could not sell those coins except for national security, when required by law or a court, or to return assets to crime victims.

The bill also creates a Proof of Reserve system. Treasury would publish an annual report on total holdings, transactions and control of private keys, checked by an independent auditor with expertise in cryptographic attestations, while the Government Accountability Office would provide oversight.

States could choose to store their own bitcoin in segregated accounts inside the federal reserve, keeping title to the coins and the right to withdraw them.

According to recent reports, the committee rewrote the bill before reporting it. Begich’s introduced text asked Treasury and Commerce to study funding bitcoin purchases with surplus remittances from Federal Reserve Banks or a revaluation of the Fed’s gold certificates, as well as with tax payments, tariff revenue and gifts.

In a recent development, those options are gone from the amended study, which now looks at swapping other digital assets in the stockpile, forfeitures and settlements, and partnerships with states or private entities. The amended version also states that nothing in the study authorizes borrowing, pledging government assets as collateral, new taxes or deficit spending to buy bitcoin.

The committee also amended the bill’s title to drop a reference to offsetting costs with Federal Reserve resources, and removed a section that would have required the Exchange Stabilization Fund to report its bitcoin holdings.

In a recent development, bitcoin Magazine reported on the bill’s bipartisan debut in May and on the full text revealing the 20-year lock-up in June. The reserve itself already exists under Executive Order 14233, signed in March 2025, but an executive order can be reversed by a future president, which is why Begich and his cosponsors want it in statute.

Setting up the reserve has been slow. In July, a report said Treasury and Commerce were competing over who would control it.

Begich’s bill has not received a floor vote. If it passes the House, the Senate would still need to act before it could reach the president’s desk.

Bitcoin's 90-day correlation with gold has reached its highest level on record, according to Galaxy Research data. The measure peaked at 0.56 on Oct. 22 and broke the previous record of 0.50, which Galaxy dated to Nov. 6, 2020.

It has been revealed that alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy Digital, posted about the record on X on Friday. "Bitcoin isn't digital gold? Bitcoin reaches highest correlation to gold of all time," he wrote.

Thorn shared two Galaxy Research charts together with the post. According to the charts, the 90-day correlation was at 0.54 on Nov. 23, and the 30-day correlation stood at 0.59 on the same day.

It has been revealed that in the first half of 2026, the 90-day correlation stayed near 0.1. It started to rise in July and climbed above 0.50 by early October, according to Galaxy's data. Between 2020 and 2025, the average reading was 0.11.

On Jan. 20, Galaxy CEO Mike Novogratz wrote on X that "the gold price is telling us we are losing reserve currency status at an accelerating rate." "$BTC is disappointing as it is still being met with selling," he added.

Thorn wrote about Bitcoin and gold on X in February. "Bitcoin's failure to trade like gold as part of 'the debasement trade' since Sep. '25 damaged its narrative with new entrants," he wrote. "When bitcoiners mentioned 'digital gold,' they were describing its fundamental properties, not that it's high beta to gold today," he added.

According to recent reports, on Wednesday, Galaxy published a report that withdrew its Oct. 26 call on the Bitcoin bear market. "We withdraw our call that the bear market ended in June," the report said. Thorn shared it on X with the comment, "As it turns out, the Bitcoin bear market is definitely not over.".

According to the report, Bitcoin closed the week ended Nov. 22 at $61,104 after seven straight weekly losses. Thorn wrote in the report that the level to watch was $58,525, Bitcoin's closing low from June 30. According to Thorn, a daily close below that level would mark "the start of a move to a materially lower low.".

Sources indicate that "The clock claims this bear is overdue to end; the depth says it has further to fall," the report mentioned. On Nov. 22, the bear market was 412 days old, and earlier ones lasted 163 to 406 days from high to low, according to Galaxy.

Bitcoin was down 53% from its October 2025 record at that point. In past bear markets, it lost 77% to 93%. If the June low breaks, Galaxy sees possible fresh lows at about $48,500 and $28,200.

Sources indicate that galaxy tracks 13 bottom signals, and two of them have been met so far. According to the report, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETPs held about 1.24 million BTC, down 71,339 BTC since Oct. 4.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 17, SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci asked Novogratz at the Digital Assets Forum in Upcoming York whether Bitcoin could return to $90,000 by the end of 2026. "Unlikely now," Novogratz stated. "Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," he added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The premium for protection against a Bitcoin drop nearly vanished for Friday’s options, ahead of a Deribit expiry covering about $7.5 billion in outstanding Bitcoin and Ethereum contracts.

Sources indicate that december options still priced protection against a fall, though at a discount to comparable bets on a rise, and traders may still move prices as they adjust hedges around settlement. Whether the rally lasts depends on demand for Bitcoin after those contracts expire.

A bounce as Friday’s contracts roll off would leave the question of spot demand returning for Bitcoin unanswered.

As of Nov. 26, GEX Monitor found that the premium for comparable Friday Bitcoin puts over calls had shrunk to 0.18 volatility points from 13.71 in its previous daily reading.

According to recent reports, puts offer protection against a fall, while calls give traders exposure to a rise. By Thursday morning, the two sides were priced almost evenly on that measure for Friday’s expiry.

Industry observers note that comparable puts carried premiums of 5.82 volatility points for Dec. 4, 8.10 for Dec. 11 and 6.62 for Dec. 25. All three premiums narrowed from the prior snapshot, yet each remained far wider than Friday’s.

An OptimistFi snapshot revealed the same pattern, with Friday’s put premium near 0.2 points and the Dec. 11 and Dec. 25 premiums at 6.4 and 6.9 points.

In a recent development, december puts kept a larger premium over comparable calls in the Nov. 26 options snapshot.

Of the four expiries shown, the Nov. 27 premium narrowed the most.

The two observations measure relative implied volatility. They do not measure options cash premiums, completed hedge flows or the probability of a price drop.

Compare GEX Monitor observations from Nov. 25 at 08:14 UTC and Nov. 26 at 08:10 UTC. The display indicates put implied volatility minus comparable call implied volatility for 25-delta options, the opposite sign from the reported risk reversal. Positions on the common axis use the values as published to two decimals.

The two observations measure relative implied volatility. They do not measure options cash premiums, completed hedge flows or the probability of a price drop.

It has been revealed that annualized implied volatility for Friday's options with strikes near Bitcoin’s price fell from 59.04% to 43.03% for Nov. 27, a drop of 16.01 volatility points. For Dec. 25, it fell from 51.17% to 48.21%, just 2.96 points.

Annualized at-the-money implied volatility for matching expiries in GEX Monitor’s Nov. 25 and Nov. 26 snapshots.

Industry observers note that source: GEX Monitor, Nov. 26 · · Nov. 25.

In a recent development, perpFinder’s expiry calendar showed over $6.8 billion of Bitcoin inverse options and $629.2 million of Ethereum inverse options due to settle at 08:00 UTC on Nov. 27.

The payout depends on where the settlement price lands relative to each contract’s strike.

Sources indicate that deribit’s inverse options settle financially in Bitcoin or Ethereum, depending on the contract. An option that finishes out of the money expires worthless, while an in-the-money contract pays out its intrinsic value, converted into the settlement coin.

As an option near the current price approaches expiry, even a small move can change how much a dealer needs to buy or sell to offset risk. After settlement, participants can unwind those hedges or replace them if they roll into a later expiry.

Sources indicate that A study by Dustin Weiss and co-authors found intraday Bitcoin price reversals around past Deribit expiries. The reversal was most pronounced when open interest was concentrated near the prevailing price, and estimated dealer positioning was consistent with buying into rises and selling into declines to stay hedged.

Trading activity also rose in Deribit perpetual futures and the spot venues used for settlement.

In a recent development, the Dec. 11 maturity was carrying $717.1 million in Bitcoin inverse-options open interest in PerpFinder’s Thursday collection, and falls after the Federal Reserve’s Dec. 8-9 policy meeting.

It has been revealed that further out, PerpFinder’s Thursday tally revealed $10 billion in Bitcoin inverse-options open interest for Dec. 25, about 47% more than Friday’s Bitcoin-only expiry. It gives December its own large settlement to watch alongside the higher relative price of its puts.

Farside Investors recorded over $3 billion of net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs across seven consecutive trading sessions through Nov. 25, including $453 million in the last session.

Industry observers note that daily net flows for US spot Bitcoin ETFs tracked by Farside Investors, Nov. 17-25.

Industry observers note that bitfinex’s Nov. 25 analysis described how swiftly an earlier rebound faded. After a Nov. 21 low near $55,500, Bitcoin reached $64,673 on Nov. 23 and gave back its intraday gain, finishing near $61,300.

A recovery that holds beyond the settlement window, a turn toward ETF inflows and a continued narrowing of December’s put premiums would give buyers a fuller picture.

ETF inflows would show demand returning through the funds, and cheaper December puts would show the change in options pricing had spread beyond Friday.

Switzerland is bringing Bitcoin self-custody into a global crypto tax reporting network

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cryptoslate

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 25, Switzerland’s Federal Council approved 57 potential partners for automatic exchanges of crypto tax information with Switzerland, so a Bitcoin withdrawal from a covered Swiss exchange to a hardware wallet could show up in an annual tax report.
  • The list includes every EU member state, the UK, and several G20 jurisdictions.
  • The rules are part of the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 25, Switzerland’s Federal Council approved 57 potential partners for automatic exchanges of crypto tax information with Switzerland, so a Bitcoin withdrawal from a covered Swiss exchange to a hardware wallet could show up in an annual tax report.

The list includes every EU member state, the UK, and several G20 jurisdictions. Switzerland intends to start exchanging data in 2028 with partners that want to participate and meet the OECD’s confidentiality, data security, and other requirements.

The rules are part of the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). Under the OECD standard, providers must retain the addresses tied to certain outbound transfers for at least five years so tax authorities can ask for them later.

Suppose a customer whose activity is subject to reporting withdraws 1 BTC from a covered Swiss exchange to a hardware wallet.

Under the outbound transfer rule, if the exchange doesn’t know the destination to be associated with a crypto service provider or a financial institution, the transfer can add 1 BTC and its fair market value in regular currency at the time of the transfer, net of transaction fees, to the customer’s annual outbound totals.

The reporting framework accounts for each relevant asset separately, so Bitcoin and other assets have their own totals.

A transfer to an address the exchange knows is associated with a crypto service provider or financial institution falls outside that field, though other transfer rules can still apply. A wallet the customer already controls can fall within the external-wallet rule.

Say the customer bought Bitcoin on the same exchange before withdrawing it. A qualifying purchase can appear in the report under the purchase category, and a qualifying withdrawal can appear in the transfer totals.

What a covered provider sends and what it keeps under the OECD framework.

Under CARF, tax authorities can request a destination address separately from the annual report.

Recent findings suggest that applies to qualifying outbound transfers of relevant crypto assets for reportable customers to destinations the provider does not know to be associated with a virtual asset service provider or financial institution. Exchange with foreign partners depends on activation and eligibility. The five-year label is the OECD minimum.

It has been revealed that maps OECD CARF Section II(A)(3)(i) and Section III(D)(3) alongside Article 15 of the Swiss tax information exchange act. Arrows show the route of information.

Sources indicate that applies to qualifying outbound transfers of relevant crypto assets for reportable customers to destinations the provider does not know to be associated with a virtual asset service provider or financial institution. Exchange with foreign partners depends on activation and eligibility. The five-year label is the OECD minimum.

Industry observers note that the reporting framework pairs transaction data with identifying information. Subject to the applicable exceptions, that information includes a customer’s name, mailing address, tax residence, taxpayer identification number and, for individuals, date of birth.

The transaction fields cover qualifying purchases, sales, swaps and transfers.

Recent findings suggest that the automatic report covers transactions the provider handles, so later movements between two private wallets without the provider’s involvement fall outside that provider’s report. The required fields omit private keys, seed phrases and full self-custody wallet balances.

Swiss law sets a longer retention period for covered compliance records. Article 17a of the Federal Act on the International Automatic Exchange of Information in Tax Matters requires covered providers to keep records and supporting documents created or obtained to meet their CARF and Swiss statutory obligations.

It refers to Article 958f of the Swiss Code of Obligations, which sets a ten-year retention period.

The Federal Council’s explanation of the legislation confirms the ten-year Swiss period when discussing CARF recordkeeping. Article 17a defines covered records by their role in meeting the provider’s obligations. It does not spell out how the ten-year period applies to individual wallet addresses.

Switzerland’s legal basis for crypto information exchange took effect Jan. 1, 2026. Its State Secretariat for International Finance says the crypto provisions do not apply in 2026 and that Jan. 1, 2027 is the earliest implementation date.

Under the Swiss filing rule, reporting providers have six months after the relevant calendar year ends to submit their reports to the Federal Tax Administration. The Swiss authority then forwards the information to eligible foreign counterparts under the applicable agreement.

If implementation begins in 2027, providers would collect that year’s data and submit it in 2028, when the first cross-border exchanges are planned.

For a reportable customer, a qualifying transfer in the first collection year could be in the record before anything is sent abroad. Keeping the withdrawal date, amount, and destination alongside the exchange record can help reconcile that transfer with other activity involving the same Bitcoin.

  • Data from Mempool.space indicated that the adjustment took effect at 05:17 UTC at block 977,760, raising mining difficulty from 134.82 trillion to 145.09 trillion.
  • Since expected mining rewards per unit of computing power move inversely to difficulty, the increase reduces what Bitcoin miners can expect to earn from their existing machines by 7.08%, assuming average transaction fees remain unchanged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that bitcoin's mining difficulty rose 7.61% on Nov. 27, intensifying financial pressure on miners already switching off machines.

Data from Mempool.space indicated that the adjustment took effect at 05:17 UTC at block 977,760, raising mining difficulty from 134.82 trillion to 145.09 trillion.

Since expected mining rewards per unit of computing power move inversely to difficulty, the increase reduces what Bitcoin miners can expect to earn from their existing machines by 7.08%, assuming average transaction fees remain unchanged.

From a starting price of $60,000, Bitcoin would need to climb approximately 7.61% to $64,570 for miners to restore their previous gross dollar revenue.

Industry observers note that bitcoin mining difficulty rose 7.61% on Nov. 27. The chart holds hashrate and block rewards fixed.

At unchanged fees, the modeled price rise of about 7.61% would restore expected gross mining revenue to its pre-reset level.

Illustrative expected gross revenue per unit of hashrate. The comparison holds subsidy and average fees in BTC per block fixed. Actual payouts and operating costs vary.

Sources indicate that divide old difficulty (134,823,837,323,273) by new difficulty (145,088,938,867,954) for a revenue index of 92.924959 at unchanged price, with average fees and subsidy fixed. Reverse that ratio for the price multiplier (1.076137). Graphic labels are rounded.

Recent findings suggest that illustrative expected gross revenue per unit of hashrate. The comparison holds subsidy and average fees in BTC per block fixed. Actual payouts and operating costs vary.

Industry observers note that friday's adjustment reverses much of the relief miners received on Nov. 14, when mining difficulty fell 9.1%, and comes as deteriorating mining economics are already forcing operators to switch off machines.

Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode reported that Bitcoin's network hashrate had fallen 8% year over year, marking its first annual contraction since China's 2021 mining ban.

While regulatory intervention forced miners offline in 2021, Glassnode attributed the current contraction to falling Bitcoin prices and record-low hashprice, a measure of the revenue miners generate per unit of computing power.

Data from Luxor's Hashrate Index showed that hashprice fell to $29.36 per petahash per day on Nov. 23, even as Bitcoin's seven-day average hashrate recovered 7.8% to 1,033 exahashes per second.

That short-term recovery in computing power helped drive Friday's difficulty increase, further compressing revenue for operators already contending with historically weak mining economics.

With Bitcoin's block subsidy fixed at 3.125 BTC, higher transaction fees could help miners offset the decline in revenue.

However, Mempool.space data indicated that transaction fees averaged just 0.0265 BTC per block across the 128 blocks mined in the 24 hours preceding Friday's adjustment, accounting for less than 1% of mining rewards.

At an unchanged Bitcoin price, average transaction fees would need to increase roughly tenfold to 0.2664 BTC per block to offset the difficulty increase.

It has been revealed that an unusually long block interval on Nov. 26 illustrates the scale of that challenge.

Alex Thorn, Galaxy Digital's head of research, noted that Bitcoin went 98 minutes and 19 seconds without producing a block, its longest interval since July and its 69th longest since 2011.

When Foundry USA eventually mined block 977,698, it processed 3,723 transactions and collected 0.1562 BTC in transaction fees.

Despite being nearly six times the average recorded before Friday's difficulty adjustment, those fees fell approximately 41% short of what miners would now need to earn consistently per block to restore their previous revenue at an unchanged Bitcoin price.

With transaction fees contributing so little to mining revenue, operators remain heavily dependent on a Bitcoin price recovery. A prolonged period of depressed prices could accelerate machine shutdowns, extending the network's annual hashrate contraction ahead of its next difficulty adjustment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bit Digital sold $50 million in Ethereum to repay a loan that helped finance its AI infrastructure expansion, but its remaining debt leaves the company's crypto treasury exposed to further financial pressure.
  • The Ethereum treasury manufacturer disclosed on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that the sale marks a reversal of Bit Digital's original financing strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bit Digital sold $50 million in Ethereum to repay a loan that helped finance its AI infrastructure expansion, but its remaining debt leaves the company's crypto treasury exposed to further financial pressure.

The Ethereum treasury manufacturer disclosed on Nov. 25 that it sold 29,825 ETH between Nov. 15 and 23 at an average price of $1,676, using the proceeds to halve its outstanding debt to Galaxy Digital to $50 million.

Industry observers note that the sale marks a reversal of Bit Digital's original financing strategy. The company borrowed against its Ethereum holdings to help fund the expansion of its AI infrastructure subsidiary, WhiteFiber, while retaining exposure to ETH.

However, Bit Digital does not expect WhiteFiber to fully repay its bridge loan until the second quarter of 2027, while its agreement with Galaxy allows the lender to demand additional collateral within 24 hours.

Bit Digital borrowed against staked ETH to fund its AI infrastructure subsidiary.

The WhiteFiber bridge remained outstanding after Bit Digital paid down its Galaxy loan.

The filings leave draw-specific recall terms and collateral thresholds undisclosed.

It has been revealed that the arrows show the direction of the original lending. The bars share a $100 million principal scale and compare Bit Digital’s reported Galaxy balances immediately before and after the November repayment.

The filings leave draw-specific recall terms and collateral thresholds undisclosed.

Kairos Research found that the value of the Ethereum collateral backing Bit Digital's $100 million Galaxy loan had fallen to about 131% of the outstanding principal as the organization began moving ETH for sale.

The research firm tracked approximately 24,800 ETH moving through Galaxy's hot wallet into Coinbase deposit addresses before Bit Digital publicly confirmed the sale, which ultimately accounted for around 18% of its Ethereum treasury.

During the period in which Galaxy delivered the ETH to Coinbase, Bit Digital's shares fell 15%, compared with a 4% decline in Ethereum.

Following the repayment, Bit Digital reported holdings of approximately 134,532 ETH and ETH equivalents, including 69,089 LsETH pledged against its remaining Galaxy debt and 36,811 ETH staked directly on Ethereum.

The pledged LsETH represents a substantial portion of the manufacturer's remaining treasury, leaving its financial position sensitive to further declines in Ethereum's price.

Under the master loan agreement, Galaxy can demand additional collateral when the value of pledged assets falls below an agreed threshold.

Bit Digital ordinarily has 24 hours from the issuance of that notice to provide additional collateral, although individual loan terms can impose shorter deadlines.

The organization's quarterly filing also disclosed that its outstanding Galaxy borrowing at the end of September was callable on seven days' notice. The repayment announcement did not specify whether that provision applies to the remaining $50 million.

These obligations leave Bit Digital potentially needing to raise capital well before WhiteFiber returns the money it borrowed.

WhiteFiber's ability to repay its parent company could depend partly on its progress securing funding for the NC-1 data center.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 9, WhiteFiber subsidiaries entered into a $300 million project financing agreement with a lender group represented by Morgan Stanley Senior Funding.

The agreement provides an initial $200 million facility, with funding conditions including operational readiness and customer acceptance of the data center's first 40 megawatts of capacity. WhiteFiber reported that no loans had been funded as of Nov. 10.

Access to the remaining $100 million requires further operational and financial milestones, including delivering financial statements covering the first three full calendar months after delivery.

The financing timetable leaves Bit Digital managing its Ethereum-backed debt while WhiteFiber works to unlock capital tied to progress on its infrastructure development.

#224933. Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1746 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety.
  • But that simple statement also hides something important.
  • According to recent reports, not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

But that simple statement also hides something important. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a new generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

According to recent reports, not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

It has been revealed that obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

Sources indicate that around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

Alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Then there are the bikes themselves.

Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

That’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

Industry observers note that to put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

According to recent reports, someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

Industry observers note that for years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

This isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

Recent findings suggest that battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

Sources indicate that for decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly rapidly into larger machines. Often though, upcoming riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely latest generation on electric two-wheelers.

Kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

According to recent reports, A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

Recent findings suggest that there’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

The rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

They’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

It has been revealed that and electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

But that’s not really my argument.

According to recent reports, my argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more vital, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

In a recent development, I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

Recent findings suggest that what excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

I bought a motorcycle around age 60 after considering the risk factors I could control:.

In a recent development, I took a MSF basic riding course before buying the motorcycle. Best investment in the whole saga.

In a recent development, I never rode impaired. That was easy.

I always rode with full protection. That was doable but inconvenient and seriously uncomfortable in hot weather.

I never rode in rainy weather or at night. Again possible but limited my use of the motorcycle for commuting. Eventually my schedule changed to evening and stopped my motorcycle commuting altogether.

According to recent reports, after a few close calls I started avoiding roads with more than one lane in each direction. That added quite a bit to my commute time.

I never rode when I was in a hurry. That meant more days I didn't use the motorcycle for commuting.

In a recent development, none of these precautions have anything to do with electric drive. After I sold my gas motorcycle I test rode an electric motorcycle and loved it. However I didn't buy it because it didn't reduce any of the risks and I wouldn't ride it more than the gas bike.

It’s that electrification could help create a latest category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.

Polo Trend. Deliveries for the sporty GTI version are expected to be around seven months.

“We clearly planned too conservatively,” a VW manager told Edison during an interview. While VW expected about 90 to 95% to choose to lease, the leasing rate is only about 50%.

The larger 52 kWh battery version has also seen higher-than-expected demand, while 90% surprisingly opted to buy the optional €810 ($890) detachable towbar.

As a result, the company is prioritizing higher-margin models, which is likely leading to longer delivery times for the base ID. Polo.

The entry-level variants “just clog up to the line,” Volkswagen’s manager remarked during the recent interview.

According to recent reports, demand for the ID. Cross, the electric equivalent to Volkswagen’s T-Cross, is also already exceeding expectations.

Cross Life with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, starting at £26,985 ($35,500).

According to recent reports, volkswagen’s newly introduced entry-level electric cars are off to a promising start. The electric urban car family, which includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, and the CUPRA Raval and Skoda Epiq, has received nearly 150,000 orders combined since production began in June.

Recent findings suggest that however, the German automaker is still facing an uphill battle. The VW Group posted an operating loss of 5.9 billion euros ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its worst quarterly loss since the Dieselgate scandal.
